analysis.one_liner: Bans large investors from cold-calling homeowners to buy their homes for six months after a declared disaster.
analysis.headline: Sen. Schiff's bill to stop institutional investors from soliciting home purchases in disaster zones was introduced and referred to committee, with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: After the federal government declares a major disaster, companies or individuals that own 75 or more single-family homes would be barred for six months from mailing, calling, or otherwise soliciting offers to buy any property in the disaster zone. The aim is to keep large landlords from swooping in while disaster-area residents are displaced, desperate, or still assessing damage, so owners can rebuild or sell on normal terms instead of under pressure. The bill amends the Stafford Act, the federal disaster-relief law, and was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in federally declared disaster areas, especially people who are displaced, repairing damage, or facing temporary income loss and might otherwise accept a lowball unsolicited offer from a big landlord. Neighborhoods where owner-occupancy is eroded when investors buy up homes after a crisis also benefit, since fewer homes get pulled into the single-family rental pool during the recovery window.

how_it_helps.text: For six months after a major disaster declaration, entities that own 75 or more single-family homes cannot make offers to purchase property in the affected area through mail, wire, or any other solicitation or contact, removing high-pressure purchase pitches while residents recover. [S2]
The ban applies to offers made directly or indirectly through any method of contact, covering the mass-mail and call campaigns that target distressed homeowners after floods, fires, and storms. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Institutional investors and large landlords that own 75 or more single-family homes lose a six-month window to acquire property in disaster areas, a period when acquisition prices are often lowest. Some homeowners who want to sell quickly to a cash buyer right after a disaster would have fewer ready buyers soliciting them, though they could still sell on the open market or to smaller buyers, who are not covered by the ban.

drawbacks.text: The six-month window is fixed regardless of how long recovery actually takes; in slow recoveries, investor solicitation could resume while many residents are still displaced. [S2]

Homeowners facing urgent cash needs right after a disaster would lose a source of unsolicited cash offers; the bill does not provide any alternative relief to help people hold their homes through the recovery period. [S2]

A good-faith objection from investors is that unsolicited offers sometimes give sellers who cannot afford repairs or insurance hikes a needed exit, and that banning them removes one option without addressing underlying disaster-recovery costs. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, well-documented practice: large investors soliciting purchase offers in disaster areas while owners are vulnerable. Its main limitation is that it is a narrow tool with a short window; it does not help homeowners afford recovery, and it relies entirely on the 75-home ownership threshold to define who is covered. On its own terms it plausibly protects disaster-zone homeowners at modest cost to large landlords, but it is a shield against one tactic rather than a solution to post-disaster displacement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it sits with no cosponsors and no floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Adam Schiff introduced the Stop Post-Disaster Vultures Act on March 2, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. [S1]
No further action appears in the record since the referral. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no action taken, the status quo holds: large single-family rental investors retain full freedom to solicit purchases in disaster areas, and no company has had to change its practices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large investors; the bill went nowhere

for.name: Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; it was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No other senators have signed on and no committee or floor action has occurred, so the partisan shape of any eventual fight is unknown.

industries.industry: Institutional owners of single-family rental homes
industries.note: The bill blocks companies and individuals owning 75 or more single-family homes from soliciting purchases in disaster zones for six months, cutting off an acquisition window when prices and seller leverage are typically lowest. For ordinary people this removes high-pressure unsolicited offers during recovery; for the industry it removes cheap inventory.

industries.industry: Main Street homeowners and local housing markets in disaster areas
industries.note: Owners keep unsolicited purchase pitches out of their mailboxes during the six months after a disaster declaration, and fewer homes shift from owner-occupied to corporate rental during recovery. Homeowners can still sell on the open market or to smaller buyers, who are not covered.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced without cosponsors and left pending in committee rarely reach a floor vote; unless the Homeland Security Committee schedules action or the disaster-investor issue becomes a legislative priority, this bill is likely to die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
